articles.title: A rare I.M. Pei-designed Texas mansion goes on sale for $22 million for the first time since 1969; the 19,133-square-foot estate has three kitchens, two wine cellars and a glass-roofed garden room
articles.summary: A unique Fort Worth estate in Texas, designed by I.M. Pei, has hit the market for $22 million.
articles.body: A unique Fort Worth estate in Texas, designed by I.M. Pei, has hit the market for $22 million. This is the first time the landmark property in Westover Hills has been offered for sale since it was constructed in 1969, according to Realtor.com. The property is listed by Madeline Jobst, Ralph Randall and Ashley Mooring of Briggs Freeman Sotheby's International Realty.One of only three private residences designed by I.M. PeiThe 19,133-square-foot mansion in Westover Hills is one of only three private homes designed by the late Chinese-American architect I.M. Pei during his lifetime. Westover House is “the last and the greatest”, according to the listing on Sotheby's. “It is one of the most significant achievements in American residential architecture.” The house reflects the design style of Pritzker Prize winner Pei’s famous works, including the Louvre Pyramid in Paris and the East Building of the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C.The sprawling home sits on nearly four acres atop a hill in Fort Worth’s exclusive Westover Hills neighbourhood. Pei, known for his modernist style, designed marvellous structures across the globe, but private homes were rare for him. The architect died in 2019 at the age of 102. His Texas work also includes the Morton H. Meyerson Symphony Center in Dallas, which many people in the region know well. The Fort Worth house follows the same approach, with clean lines, concrete walls and large windows that bring the outdoors inside.Westover House was built as a family homeWestover House was built for Anne Burnett Tandy, an oil heiress, and her husband, Charles Tandy. Charles led a company that started as a leather goods business and grew into a large retail operation. It later acquired RadioShack. Charles Tandy died in 1978, and Anne passed away two years later. The home was then passed to their daughter, Anne Marion, who lived there until her death in 2020. The Tandy family still owns the property, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal.Inside the houseBuilt in 1969, the house spans 19,133 sq ft and features a unique layout with museum-inspired interiors, a soaring glass-roofed garden room, an art gallery, a luxurious primary suite and a wellness retreat.“At the heart of Westover House is the garden room: a soaring, light-filled space. Its canted roof of glass and steel rises above the tree line, and Pei carried its triangular geometry throughout the house, repeating the slope in four smaller angled peaks that serve as ‘light grabbers’ – north-facing glass panels that pull natural light deep into the living spaces from morning through dusk,” the listing says.The single-storey home has seven bedrooms and three kitchens. Its thick concrete walls are made with rose-quartz granite from Colorado, with all the textured lines carved by hand. Portuguese marble and Burmese teak flooring run throughout the rooms. The outdoor terraces are finished in granite.There are two formal living areas and two formal dining areas on either side of the garden room. Each has a large and a small room connected to one another, making the spaces ideal for entertaining.The art gallery is a spacious hall off the garden room that connects to the private part of the house. The primary suite features a large bedroom with a sitting area, a study area, a private bathroom and ample closet space. It also has a library, a fireplace and a wet bar, along with an adjoining second bedroom with its own bathroom and a large closet.There are two additional bedrooms and bathrooms in the guest quarters. The house also has a cocktail bar, three fireplaces, a den, an office/study in the private wing, a wellness room and an elevator. The large basement houses two climate-controlled wine cellars, while a separate laundry room and a staff area with two bathrooms complete the home.Outside, the 3.86-acre lot includes a heated pool, a putting green and a six-car garage with a carport for four cars.According to the listing, Westover House is more than an architectural triumph. “It is a Fort Worth legend.” Interior designers including Melanie Kahane, Benjamin Baldwin, Ron Bradshaw, Valliant Interiors and Windfohr Design have worked on the house.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Barbra Streisand donated $10 million to Cedars-Sinai’s women’s heart center; in 2026, the center bearing her name is leading a new $7.5 million NIH-funded five-year study on women’s aging
articles.summary: Aging is rarely a single-system story. The heart, brain, muscles and blood vessels change together, yet medical research has often studied them separately.
articles.body: Aging is rarely a single-system story. The heart, brain, muscles and blood vessels change together, yet medical research has often studied them separately. A new five-year research project at Cedars-Sinai is taking a broader view, investigating whether damage to the body’s smallest blood vessels could help explain several health challenges women face as they grow older.Backed by a $7.5 million grant from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the National Institute on Aging (NIA), the study brings together specialists in cardiovascular health, neurology, biostatistics and frailty research. At its centre is a question with implications far beyond cardiology: could understanding tiny blood vessels reveal new ways to protect the ageing heart, brain and body?Looking beyond the heartThe research is being led by investigators at the Smidt Heart Institute’s Barbra Streisand Women’s Heart Center, named after the legendary singer and actor following her $10 million donation to Cedars-Sinai.The new initiative, known as the Microvascular Aging Effects—Women’s Evaluation of Systemic Aging Tenacity in Heart, Brain and Frailty study, or MAE-WEST HBF, has been established as a Specialized Center of Research Excellence on Sex Differences through the NIH Office of Research on Women’s Health. Its focus is the microvasculature: the network of tiny blood vessels that delivers oxygen and nutrients throughout the body. Researchers want to understand how deterioration in these vessels may connect not only to cardiovascular disease but also to cognitive decline and reduced physical strength.A trail of cluesThe project builds on years of work at Cedars-Sinai examining coronary microvascular disease, a condition that affects the smallest blood vessels supplying the heart and is more common in women.Previous research from the Barbra Streisand Women’s Heart Center has linked small-vessel disease, chronic inflammation and iron accumulation with impaired function in the heart, brain and kidneys, alongside declining physical strength.That history gives the new study a strong foundation. Rather than examining individual conditions in isolation, researchers will explore whether they share underlying biological pathways.The distinction is important because women can experience cardiovascular symptoms that are less obvious than the classic signs associated with heart disease. Microvascular disease has historically been overlooked or mistaken for other conditions, leaving some patients without appropriate diagnosis or treatment.Connecting heart, brain and mobilityMAE-WEST HBF brings together a multidisciplinary team to investigate what happens beyond the cardiovascular system. Neurology researchers at Cedars-Sinai will examine the relationship between small-vessel damage and brain health, while collaborators at UCLA will handle biostatistical analysis. Researchers at the University of Texas at Arlington will focus on frailty and physical function.The ambition is to understand whether a problem in the smallest vessels can set off a wider chain of age-related changes.If researchers can establish those connections, the findings could eventually influence how doctors screen for risk and identify people who may be vulnerable to several conditions at once.Rethinking healthy ageingWomen generally live longer than men, but longevity does not necessarily mean more years in good health. Women also experience higher rates of chronic illness, meaning a longer lifespan can include more time living with disability or declining function.That makes prevention particularly important. The researchers envision a future where healthy ageing involves earlier screening, better imaging and more personalised preventive care, identifying biological risks before they develop into major disease.The study also reflects a broader shift in women's health research: moving away from treating individual organs as separate systems and towards understanding how the body ages as a whole.After decades of research into women's cardiovascular health, the latest initiative aims to connect three crucial measures of wellbeing healthy heart, a functioning brain and the ability to remain physically strong and independent.Images Courtesy: Wikipedia and istockYou use AI every day. articles.title: 'Could not prevent regime change within own party': Devendra Fadnavis mocks Uddhav Thackeray
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis on Sunday hit back at former chief minister Uddhav Thackeray for backing calls for a “regime
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis on Sunday hit back at former chief minister Uddhav Thackeray for backing calls for a “regime change” in India, saying the Shiv Sena (UBT) president had failed to prevent a regime change within his own party.Also Read | ‘Taking away right to vote, protest’: Uddhav backs opposition's ‘regime change’ call against government“First of all, Uddhav Thackeray could not prevent a regime change within his own Shiv Sena, so I do not know what other regime change he is talking about. The moment his party abandoned Hindutva and the ideology of Hindu Hriday Samrat Balasaheb Thackeray, such turmoil erupted within the party that those who wanted to follow Balasaheb Thackeray’s principles formed the real Shiv Sena,” Fadnavis told reporters in Nagpur.Fadnavis was referring to the June 2022 split in the undivided Shiv Sena, which led to the formation of two factions led by Uddhav Thackeray and Maharashtra deputy chief Minister Eknath Shinde.The chief minister asserted that any regime change in India could take place only through elections, not through street protests.“I have made it very clear: Stop fighting against the Constitution of India. Decisions in this country will be taken in Parliament and in accordance with the Constitution, not on the streets. In a democracy, governments are decided through elections,” he said.Fadnavis expressed confidence that Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government would return to power in 2029 and called on the opposition to win public support to secure an electoral victory.“Today, Narendra Modi’s government is in power, and it will be elected again. But if you want a regime change, you must contest elections, win the hearts of the people and secure an electoral victory. Those who dream of bringing about a regime change in India by disregarding the Constitution, as witnessed in Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Pakistan, will never succeed in their intentions,” the chief minister added, referring to the youth- and student-led movements that toppled incumbent governments in three of India’s neighbouring countries in recent years.Fadnavis’ comments came a day after Uddhav Thackeray backed recent calls by activists and opposition leaders for a regime change in India, arguing that denying people the right to express their views through elections and protests would leave them with no option but to seek a change of government.“If you take away our right to express our views through elections and protest, then we're standing up just to overthrow this government,” the Shiv Sena (UBT) chief said.The remarks come amid a political row over references to regime change by opposition leaders and student activists during ongoing protests in Delhi against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.Senior advocate Prashant Bhushan, student activist and All India Students Association (AISA) president Neha Bora, and Congress spokesperson Pawan Khera have publicly used or discussed the phrase “regime change” at conferences and press briefings in connection with the protests.(with ANI inputs)Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: At Louisiana’s Fort Polk, researchers spread pulverized classified paper on damaged Army land; native plant cover was 48% higher at one soil site and 42% higher at another
articles.summary: Researchers at Fort Polk, Louisiana, find that pulverized classified paper boosts native plant growth by 45% on military training lands, offering a sustainable solution for soil rehabilitation.
articles.body: Researchers at Fort Polk, Louisiana, investigated whether pulverised classified paper waste could help restore military training land. Military training grounds can experience soil disturbance from movement of vehicles and soldiers across the land, making vegetation establishment more difficult. The US Agricultural Research Service (ARS) reported that native plant cover was 45% higher on plots receiving the recommended paper treatment compared to control plots. The experiment examined whether shredded paper could serve as a soil amendment while providing an alternative use for waste otherwise sent to landfill. The findings were published in 2019 in Soil and Tillage Research, wherein researchers recommended applying pulverised paper at 35.9 metric tonnes per hectare.How researchers tested the paper amendmentThe field experiment began in April 2015, when researchers spread pulverised paper obtained from document-shredding facilities across experimental plots and incorporated it into the upper 15 centimetres of soil. They then planted four native warm-season grasses: big bluestem, Indiangrass, little bluestem and switchgrass.The experiment used two soil types; the first was an Alfisol, taken from more fertile soil conditions at one site, while the second was an Ultisol, which had lower fertility. Different quantities of paper were then applied at each location, and the results were compared to untreated control plots and plots that were treated with conventional soil.The rates differed because the researchers encountered difficulties incorporating the highest application levels into the Alfisol soil. The Ultisol plots received rates of 17.9, 35.9, 53.8 and 71.7 metric tonnes per hectare, and the rates at the Alfisol site were 9.0, 17.9, 26.9 and 35.9 metric tonnes per hectare. Consequently, 71.7 metric tonnes per hectare was the highest rate tested at the Ultisol site.The conventional treatment consisted of lime, applied at 2,240 kilograms per hectare, and nitrogen fertiliser at 56 kilograms of nitrogen per hectare. The control plots received neither amendment nor fertiliser, although they were prepared and seeded in the same way as the other plots.Different soil conditions produced different resultsThe scientific paper provides the site-specific figures behind the findings, and at the Alfisol site, native plant cover at 35.9 metric tonnes per hectare was 48% higher than the control and 62% higher than the conventional treatment. Conversely, at the Ultisol site, native plant cover at 71.7 metric tonnes per hectare, the highest rate tested there, was 42% higher than the control and 17% higher than the conventional treatment.In terms of plant cover and plant biomass, different results were also produced. At the Ultisol site, native plant biomass at 71.7 metric tonnes per hectare was 71% lower than the control, while the conventional treatment produced 355% more. At the Alfisol site, native plant biomass at 35.9 metric tonnes per hectare was 90% higher than the control and 96% higher than the conventional treatment. These measurements indicate that greater plant cover did not necessarily mean greater plant biomass across both sites.The researchers linked the contrasting responses to differences in nutrient availability. The Ultisol site showed improvements in certain physical and chemical soil properties, but its low fertility meant that nitrogen immobilisation could constrain grass growth. At the more fertile Alfisol site, the carbon-rich paper tied up nitrogen, which helped reduce competition from weeds and invasive plants and favoured the planted native grasses. ARS also reported estimated savings of about $11,600 per hectare and annual savings of around $20,000 per military facility, alongside a potential diversion of about 64 metric tonnes of paper from landfill. Subsequently, the Corps of Engineers produced a user guide based on the research to help military facilities consider the approach to land rehabilitation.You use AI every day.
